description: Hi, I'm Ughur, a 16-year-old from Istanbul passionate about space biology. I've independently analyzed NASA’s GeneLab data on spaceflight gene expression, gaining strong analytical skills. I bring solid scientific framing to a team and am looking for teammates skilled in coding, UI/UX, or data visualization to build a space/biology project together!
summary: AstroCura is an offline-first health co-pilot for astronauts on missions where Mission Control is minutes away. It learns each crew member's own baseline from sleep, mood, stress, reaction time, heart rate, HRV, blood pressure, body mass, exercise, temperature, SpO₂, cabin CO₂ and radiation dose, then flags sustained drift with robust statistics (a leaky CUSUM) instead of population ranges. Indicators are organised by NASA's five human-spaceflight hazards, and cross-hazard rules turn drift into plain-language findings such as illness, sleep restriction or cardiovascular deconditioning, with the evidence shown. Because communication delay on a Mars mission grows to many minutes each way, triage adapts: act now, call ground, or send a compact downlink packet and keep working the onboard protocol. The demo runs entirely in the browser on a clearly labelled synthetic Mars-transit mission and includes real NASA OSDR Inspiration4 blood-count data. A stress-test lab lets anyone inject a problem into a simulated crew member and see how many days AstroCura needed to notice, and how often it misses. It is decision support, not a diagnostic device.
details:
THE PROBLEM

Long missions expose astronauts to radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity and a hostile closed environment. NASA's Human Research Program treats these five hazards as coupled. On a Mars mission the delay to the ground reaches many minutes each way, so Mission Control's real-time view of crew health fades and astronauts must spot changes in themselves. The challenge asks for software that gathers health indicators and lets astronauts evaluate and act on their health status.

WHAT WE BUILT

A single-file web app (no server, no account, no network calls), about 230 KB, with nine views: (1) Overview: a plain-language headline for the selected day, one row per NASA hazard, ranked findings with evidence, radiation budget, and a short section on where the same idea could help on Earth (framed as possible, not tested). (2) Trends: any indicator against the person's own baseline band, plus a sustained-drift score. (3) Crew of four: four simulated crew members with different personal normals (an endurance athlete with a resting heart rate near 47 bpm, a long sleeper, a person with higher blood pressure, and the Mars-scenario commander), each with one injected drift, shown on one shared scale with the personal band, a fixed placeholder limit, when AstroCura flagged each person and when the fixed limit fired. (4) Actions and downlink: crew action list, a communication-delay selector (LEO, Moon, Mars close approach, Mars far side) that changes the triage advice, a compact downlink packet (text and about 1 KB JSON), and a printable flight-surgeon report. (5) Check-in and data: add a day, import or export CSV, switch datasets. (6) Stress test: pick an indicator, size, start day and onset; a fresh simulated crew member is generated, AstroCura reports its Watch and Alert days next to a fixed-limit alarm, then repeats the same problem on 40 other simulated crew members (median delay, how many it missed, false Watches). (7) NASA OSDR data: real Inspiration4 blood counts. (8) Method: hazard to HRP risk to indicator mapping, parameters, data provenance, limitations, references. (9) Validation: Monte-Carlo false-alarm and detection-delay results, re-runnable in the browser.

INNOVATION

1. Personal baselines, not population ranges. Each indicator is compared with the crew member's own first 28 days (median and robust spread). On the real OSDR data, people differ from one another by up to about 3 times more than they vary within themselves for red-cell count, haematocrit, haemoglobin, monocytes and platelets, so one population range fits nobody well.

2. Explainable cross-hazard reasoning. Rules combine drifting indicators into named patterns (illness, sleep restriction with performance impact, cardiovascular deconditioning, cabin air, radiation event) and show the evidence behind each.

3. Delay-aware triage. The recommended response depends on the one-way delay. Critical findings: act onboard and notify ground at once. Alerts: call ground only if the delay is about a minute or less, otherwise send the packet and keep working the protocol.

4. Offline and private by design. It runs on the habitat computer; crew data leaves only when the crew sends a packet.

5. It shows where it fails. The stress test lets judges or crew break a simulated crew member on purpose and see the misses as well as the catches. For example a 2-sigma sleep loss (0.9 h per night) is noticed in a median of about 9 days, is missed entirely in a few of 40 simulated crew members, and a fixed 3.5 h limit never fires.

METHOD

Robust personal baseline (median + 1.4826 x MAD, with a noise floor), adverse-direction z-score, evidence scaled by each indicator's own lag-1 autocorrelation, a leaky one-sided CUSUM for sustained drift plus a single-day spike test, rule-based pattern insights, and hard absolute limits that override everything. Domain readiness = 100 - 25 x mean positive smoothed adverse z; overall = 0.5 x weakest domain + 0.5 x mean.

DATA: WHAT IS REAL, WHAT IS NOT

REAL: Inspiration4 complete blood counts from NASA OSDR (OSD-569), four crew members, used only in the NASA OSDR tab. NASA-published values: hazard and risk taxonomy (HRP); about 1.8 mSv/day cruise dose rate from Curiosity RAD (Zeitlin et al. 2013), which sets the simulated dose baseline; astronauts average roughly 6 h sleep against 8.5 h scheduled (Barger et al. 2014, NASA-funded), which sets the simulated sleep baseline. SIMULATED: every daily value in the Mars-transit scenario, the injected events (solar particle event, sleep restriction, exercise decline, illness, CO2 scrubber degradation) and the communication-delay curve. Public daily crew data does not exist, so the simulation gives us ground truth to test against. The app labels it SIMULATED DATA on every screen. ASSUMED: typical resting physiology and spreads, hard limits (placeholders for a mission's medical requirements), and the wording of crew actions.

TESTING AND VALIDATION (all on synthetic data; not clinical validation)

False alarms (healthy crew member, 180 days, 400 simulated missions each): with independent daily noise, 11.3% of missions show any Watch and 1.0% any Alert; with autocorrelated noise (rho = 0.25) 27.8% and 3.0%. Detection delay (sustained shift starting day 40; four indicators; 200 missions per cell): with independent noise a 2-sigma shift reaches Watch in a median of 6-7 days (90th percentile 19-23 days) and is missed in 2-4% of runs; Alert takes a median of 12-14 days and is missed in 10-17%. With realistic autocorrelated noise (rho = 0.25) the 2-sigma Watch median is 8-9 days and 10-21% are missed; Alert is missed in 30-37%. 3-sigma shifts reach Watch in a median of 3-4 days with at most 2% missed. 1-sigma shifts are mostly not reported, by design. Mars scenario (days 29-39 healthy: nothing raised): first Watch after event start: solar particle event +0 days; illness +2; CO2 drift +10; exercise decline +22 (heart-rate variability, the first related signal, +17); sleep restriction +28. 35 automated engine tests pass. The UI was tested across all nine tabs on desktop and phone widths with no console errors; axe-core (WCAG 2.2 AA) reports 0 violations on every tab and Lighthouse scores Accessibility 100, Best Practices 100 and SEO 100.

WHAT THE REAL DATA DOES AND DOES NOT SHOW

Of 132 pre-flight blood-count values, 3 (2%) fall outside the lab's population range. At R+1, 1 of 48 values is outside the lab range, and 23 of 48 are outside the person's own 2-3-sample pre-flight range. Chance alone gives about 26, so we do not claim detection or a flight effect from this: four people and 2-3 baseline samples each is far too little. What the data does support is the premise behind personal baselines: between-person spread exceeds within-person spread for several analytes.

LIMITATIONS

Not a medical device and not clinically validated; decision support for a crew member and flight surgeon only. The detector was tuned and tested on synthetic noise; real physiology adds circadian rhythm, workload, sensor dropout and microgravity adaptation. If a crew member is already drifting during the baseline window, the baseline absorbs it, so pre-flight data should seed it. The four personal normals in the Crew tab are plausible, not measured from real astronauts. Hard limits and action text are placeholders to be replaced by a mission's own procedures.

FUTURE WORK

Ingest ISS cabin telemetry and RadLab dosimetry for realistic environment and dose baselines; validate on analog missions (e.g. HERA) through formal data requests; add bone and vision modules and a ground-side flight-surgeon console.

TECHNOLOGY

Vanilla HTML/CSS/JavaScript, dependency-free; hand-built SVG charts; deterministic seeded simulator; one shared engine file used by the page and the tests. Works offline with an embedded font. Light, high-contrast interface, keyboard operable, status never shown by colour alone, reduced motion respected. Source code: https://github.com/ughurpirali/astrocura/
